newsitem.title: USA: US labor mkt tight, prices in check-Minn Fed chief.
newsitem.headline: US labor mkt tight, prices in check-Minn Fed chief.

text.p: The U.S. economy appears to be running near full employment, but job insecurity may be keeping wages and overall inflation in check, according to Gary Stern, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.

The past few years have brought "very positive news on inflation in an environment where we have had a tight labor market (and) a long period of sustained economic growth," Stern said at a breakfast at the College of St. Scholastica.
Stern said fears of job losses have helped control wage growth, and therefore price increases, over the past several years.
"Concern about job security is one of the factors that have been at work here," he said.
Asked about fiscal policy and the importance of a balanced budget, Stern said running a deficit is more harmful to the U.S. economy that it would be in other countries with higher saving rates.

"Because we are a relatively low-saving economy, when you run a budget deficit ... you are adding to the demands of the capital markets," he said. "(A budget) surplus would mean you get some government saving added to the private-sector saving."
Stern also said current high levels of consumer debt in the U.S. apparently have not damaged consumer balance sheets and do not pose an economic threat.
Stern said one of the central bank's objectives is to achieve an inflation rate low enough that it is "not a factor in economic decision making."
He added that he agreed with recent assessments that the Consumer Price Index overstates inflation.
"The CPI, at least as currently constructed, does overstate the rate of inflation," Stern said.
"The U.S. economy has clearly moved in the direction of lower inflation for a sustained period of time now," he later added.
